unsettled: Source of the Dangerous Drugs Act and the Indian Hemp Act: no government-hosted text was found, so both were read in the Policy and Legal Advocacy Centre (PLAC) compendium of the 2004 Laws of Nigeria (placng.org); the Indian Hemp Act definition was also read in FAOLEX. Every record taken from them is 'draft' although the two readings agree. The editor must decide whether to accept these copies.

NDLEA Act s. 52 defines 'Narcotic Drug' and 'Psychotropic Substances' by reference to the UN schedules, with no date and no 'as amended from time to time' wording; the enactment line ends with 1999 No. 62. If the reference is fixed, substances the UN scheduled after the Act's text are not covered. This affects every 'Covered by reference' record; the dates of UN scheduling were not read.

Codeine: s. 52 'Narcotic Drug' names only the First Schedule of the 1961 Convention, and the site's UN layer places codeine in Schedule II, so the NDLEA Act definitions do not reach it. The only Nigerian list read that names codeine is the Dangerous Drugs Act (L.N. 83 of 1955 order), read in the PLAC copy.

NAFDAC: its Narcotics page shows a 'List of controlled Drugs' with no link, and its FAQ gives only examples per category, with no legal basis printed. Items not named in the FAQ (for example esketamine, tapentadol, GBL, kratom, the new benzodiazepines) may still be on NAFDAC's full list.
Esketamine: NAFDAC names ketamine as a 'Nationally Controlled Drug'; whether that covers its S-enantiomer is not stated.

Cannabidiol: not named anywhere; whether CBD products made from the plant fall under 'Indian hemp' (plant parts, resin, preparations containing resin) or under Dangerous Drugs Act s. 8(1)(b) (extracts and tinctures) is a question of interpretation.

Dangerous Drugs Act s. 9(1) bars trade in products obtained from the phenanthrene alkaloids of opium or the ecgonine alkaloids of the coca leaf that were not in medical or scientific use on 13 July 1931, unless relaxed by order. Whether this generic clause reaches any item not named (for example a semi-synthetic opioid such as buprenorphine, if it is such a product) was not decided.

Pending law: the NDLEA's own news post of 28 May 2025 says the amended NDLEA Act had been passed by the National Assembly and was awaiting Presidential assent; no enacted amendment was found. News reports, not used as a source of fact, describe a refusal of assent in June 2025 and an 'NDLEA Bill 2026' sent to the Senate on 14 October 2026 that would repeal the NDLEA Act and the Indian Hemp Act.
